facts.text: I discuss the lack of representation of minorities in the Israeli Supreme Court and how minorities do not see themselves represented.
I say that being in the first or second Israel is a privilege.
I say I have no real savings apart from my pension.
I describe a difficult childhood during the Holocaust.
I say my parents were not allowed to work or teach in Israel.
I ask why I am considered the first Israel and not the second Israel.
I discuss the achievements of Aaron Bozgelo, a child of immigrants from Morocco.
I say a committee for selecting judges was looking to have more Arabs and Easterners and also religious and ultra-Orthodox judges.
I say the committee was looking for the best out of 70 possible judges.
I say there were only 15 Spanish judges.
I say there was no ill will or racism behind the selection and they were searching for Spaniards.
I discuss the appointment of an expert to the Supreme Court and how it was prevented.
I say the person was not worthy for appointment due to their journalistic writing in the press.
I address mistakes made during my judicial revolution and say they may have been too far-reaching, too inclusive, and too liberal for the Israeli public.
I say I have been hearing these voices since 1995 when the verdict in the United Mizrahi Bank case was given.
I say Judge Barak was warned that he was running too fast.
I say Judge Barak argued that they needed more rights and that he could not create them as a judge.
I say Judge Barak believes his position fits Israeli society, which has a history of suffering and immigrants from different countries.
I say the Knesset instructed Judge Barak to recognize the right to human dignity and that laws violating human dignity should be considered unconstitutional.
I discuss the possibility of a country where people do not want rights or a constitution.
I say I believe that if people want a dictatorship, there will be enough dictators willing to serve them.
I describe my own experiences in the Holocaust.
I say I want to keep my family in their land and have a garden in Israel.
I conclude that without a spirit of freedom and aspiration for rights, no court will be effective.
I recount being a child in Europe during the Nazi invasion.
I remember being pushed into a small neighborhood and living in a ghetto with constant hunger.
I recall playing on the street while fearing being harmed or killed by a German soldier.
I describe a central square called Democracy Square in the ghetto where all Jews were asked to enter.
I say families had to take children under 9 out on the road and put them in tour cars to be murdered in a children's action.
I describe a Jewish boy of 8-9 years old dressed as an older person and taken to his father's workplace.
I say a German officer asked the boy his age and his answer determined if he would live or die.
I describe being 12 years old in the ghetto and being challenged by the rule of law.
I say we had to find a Thai man willing to take us out.
I say we were put in a box with a German soldier sitting on top.
I say the policeman was bribed and the box was opened, allowing escape to a safe place with my mother.
I describe hiding inside a double wall in a Lithuanian village with my mother.
I say my mother taught me arithmetic, geography, and history while we were in the wall.
I say my father did not care to get us out.
I describe fleeing my home and traveling on top of a train to escape the Soviet regime.
I say I had to learn to survive and evade robbers.
I say some people saw us as academic and elite.
I discuss the end of World War II when the train stopped and horns began to blow.
I describe persecution without human rights.
I remember a Jewish brigade symbol with the Star of David.
I say a Jewish soldier saved me.
I discuss a judicial philosophy of protecting both national security and human rights.
I say national security and human rights can live together.
I discuss the importance of the state and the necessity of security procedures to protect human rights.
I mention the Law of Return granting Jews a "golden key" to enter the State of Israel.
I say I returned to Kovna and met the family that saved me during the Holocaust.
I say the family's daughter explained they took the risk because they were strict Catholics.
I discuss a large demonstration held in Israel in 1999 in response to Supreme Court decisions including the question of who is a Jew.
I say the demonstration was organized by ultra-Orthodox Jews from various factions.
I say the demonstration was attended by more than a quarter of a million people.
I say the organizers emphasized a short prayer and banners indicating opposition to the judicial dictatorship.
I say today security officials in the legal system continue to use the demonstration as an example of power.
I say I am asked how I feel when hundreds of thousands of Israelis demonstrate at my workplace.
I say I am not cold-hearted and that ultra-orthodox leaders came to me asking me not to interfere in matters of religion and state.
I say I have not sought psychological support despite pressures I faced.
I say a lawyer named Jacob Weinroth commented that my mental structure is like that of a religious person and that I dream of living in a society that rules universal values.
I say I am a soldier in the army of the law and come from an ultra-Orthodox religious family.
I say at family events the ultra-orthodox faction sees me as a demon and it hurts me.
I say the Supreme Court is supposed to be both Jewish and democratic.
I say I identify more with the Democratic Party.
I say I wish I knew more about Jewish Hebrew law and Talmud.
I say I do not think democracy should have a heavier weight than Jewishness; they are equal.
I have been in love with my wife for 70 years.
I have had the same attitude toward my wife since we first met.
I say we see ourselves as two parts of one whole and do not see ourselves living without each other.
I was very involved in the formation of our four children: Avner, Esther, Michal, and Tamar.
I have written a book about the fundamental law of human dignity and freedom that reflects Israeli law.
I say allegations of nepotism were heard against me and that it was wrong for the children of judges to intern with their fathers.
I concluded that it is better for judges not to take care of their children because it can lead to criticism.
I express sadness at Yitzhak Rabin's passing and note his honesty.
I say I resigned after Yitzhak Rabin did not require a plea deal but Netanyahu did, and that a plea deal was agreed to prevent a rift in the nation.
I say if Netanyahu had agreed to the deal at the time, I would have had to confess and resign and leave political life.
I say Alika is in old age and it is hard for me to see her in this state.
I say Alika had a wonderful life and that gives me comfort.
I have four children and 11 grandchildren.
I thank Judge Aharon Barak for having this conversation and also thank Amir Ben David and Noa Myel for helping prepare this idea.
